name: Yoga
about: Poses, flows and breathing from India that build strength, balance and calm.
safety: Practise on a non-slip mat, never force a pose, and skip anything that hurts. If you are pregnant or have a condition, ask a teacher or doctor first.
tips: Breathe through the nose and let the breath set the pace.
Little and often beats long and rare: 10 minutes a day adds up.
Soft knees are fine in folds: the spine matters more than the legs.

name: Self-defence basics
about: Awareness, a safe stance and simple, high-percentage strikes to create space and get away. Getting away safely is always the goal.
safety: Avoiding danger and getting away beat any technique. For real scenarios, take an in-person class.
tips: Notice exits and people around you; awareness prevents most trouble.
Keep open hands up in front of you: it looks calm and protects your face.
Use a loud voice; shouting 'Stop!' draws attention and help.

name: Boxing
about: Punching, footwork and defence. Shadow boxing is one of the best home workouts for cardio and coordination.
trains: Cardio, hand speed, coordination and stress relief.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Chin down, hands up, elbows in: always return to this guard.
Never fully lock the elbow when shadow boxing.
Exhale sharply with every punch.

name: Karate
about: Built on kihon (basics): stances, punches, blocks and kicks repeated with precision, then linked into kata.
trains: Precision, leg strength, focus and discipline.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Pull the opposite fist back to the hip as you punch (hikite).
Keep stances low but knees over toes.
Slow, perfect reps teach more than fast, sloppy ones.

name: Kickboxing & Muay Thai
about: Striking with fists, elbows, knees and shins. Solo drills build powerful hips and serious conditioning.
trains: Hip power, balance, core and stamina.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Pull the hands down as the knee drives up.
Pivot the standing foot on kicks to protect the knee.
Keep your guard up even when kicking.

name: Kung fu (Wushu)
about: A family of Chinese martial arts. Training starts with stances (ma bu, gong bu) that build the legs for everything else.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Hold horse stance a few seconds longer each week.
Sink your weight; don't lean forward over your toes.
Relaxed shoulders make strikes faster.

name: Kalaripayattu
about: One of the oldest surviving fighting systems, practised in the kalari of Kerala. Training starts with meippayattu, body conditioning built from flowing kicks, jumps and animal-inspired stances (vadivu), long before any weapon.
trains: Flexibility, leg strength, balance and body control.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Warm up hips and hamstrings before leg swings; height comes from flexibility, not force.
Keep the standing knee soft and the supporting foot flat for balance.
In vadivu, hold each stance and breathe slowly through the nose before moving on.

name: Kushti (Pehlwani)
about: Traditional Indian wrestling, trained in the akhara. Wrestlers are famous for bodyweight conditioning: dand (Hindu push-ups), baithak (Hindu squats) and swinging the mugdar (Indian club).
safety: Wrestling holds and throws need a coach and a mat. Solo conditioning here is safe to start: build reps slowly and keep your back neutral.
tips: Breathe out as you swoop forward in dand, in as you push back.
For baithak, let the heels rise and swing the arms for rhythm.
Traditional sets are high-rep but slow: quality before count.

name: Gatka
about: A Sikh martial art, today often shown as stick fencing with a wooden stick (soti) and small shield (farri). Its rhythmic stepping is called pentra.
trains: Footwork, reflexes, shoulder endurance and rhythm.
safety: Use a light bamboo or PVC stick, clear space around you, and start slowly. Never practise near other people or pets.
tips: Pentra comes first: step lightly in rhythm before adding strikes.
Strike from the shoulder and hips, not just the wrist.
Return the stick to guard after every strike.

name: Silambam
about: A staff art from Tamil Nadu. Practitioners learn kaaladi (footwork patterns) first, then spinning the staff in figure-eights and circles while moving.
trains: Coordination, wrist and shoulder strength, rhythm and footwork.
safety: Use a light bamboo or PVC stick, clear space around you, and start slowly. Never practise near other people or pets.
tips: Learn the footwork without the stick first; the spins follow the feet.
Grip loosely and let the wrists turn; a tight grip tires the forearms fast.
Start with slow figure-eights on each side before linking them.

name: Lathi Khela
about: Traditional stick fighting from Bengal, once taught in village akharas. Solo practice drills the basic strikes and blocks with a long bamboo lathi.
safety: Use a light bamboo or PVC stick, clear space around you, and start slowly. Never practise near other people or pets.
tips: Hold the lathi with both hands about shoulder-width apart.
Block with the middle of the stick, between your hands.
Step as you strike so the power comes from the legs.

name: Mardani Khel
about: The traditional martial art of Maharashtra, linked with the Maratha warriors and known for fast spinning of the lathi and other weapons.
safety: Use a light bamboo or PVC stick, clear space around you, and start slowly. Never practise near other people or pets.
tips: Speed is the last thing to add: smooth circles first, fast ones later.
Keep elbows close and let the forearms do the spinning.
Breathe out on each change of direction.

name: Thang-ta
about: Part of Huyen Langlon from Manipur. Thang-ta is the armed side (sword and spear); sarit-sarak is the unarmed side, with low, flowing stances and evasive footwork.
trains: Low-stance leg strength, agility and balance.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Stay low and move from the hips, keeping your head level.
Turn on the balls of your feet, not the heels.
Flow between stances slowly first; the art values smoothness over power.

name: Musti Yuddha
about: An old Indian art of unarmed combat with fists, associated with Varanasi. Practice here focuses on guard, footwork and straight strikes.
safety: Learn partner work, sparring and anything with a weapon only from a qualified teacher. This app covers solo practice: stances, footwork, shadow drills and conditioning.
tips: Hands come back to guard as fast as they go out.
Turn the back foot and hip into each rear-hand strike.
Keep strikes shoulder-high in shadow work to protect your elbows.
